questions.knowledgeNote: For a finite limit at a the function must stay bounded near a; 2/(2 + 3x) blows up as x → −2/3.
questions.question: Q1. Prove that lim (x→−2/3) 2/(2 + 3x) does not exist.
questions.solution: At x = −2/3 the denominator 2 + 3x = 0, so the expression is undefined there. Approach from the right: x = −2/3 + h with h → 0⁺ gives 2 + 3x = 3h → 0⁺, so 2/(3h) → +∞. Approach from the left: x = −2/3 − h gives 2 + 3x = −3h → 0⁻, so 2/(−3h) → −∞. The one-sided limits are not finite and not equal, hence the limit does not exist. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q1; book p483 = PDF p510

questions.knowledgeNote: A function is 'defined' at a point when substitution gives a finite real number.
questions.question: Q2(i). Is f(x) = (x − 1)/(x + 2) defined for the value x = 1?
questions.solution: f(1) = (1 − 1)/(1 + 2) = 0/3 = 0, a finite real number, and the denominator is non-zero at x = 1. So the function is defined there. Boxed Defined (matches the printed key, book p486).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q2(i); book p484 = PDF p511; key book p486 = PDF p513

questions.knowledgeNote: A zero denominator at the point means no value is assigned there, even though the limit may exist.
questions.question: Q2(ii). Is f(x) = (x³ + 1)/(x − 1) defined for the value x = 1?
questions.solution: At x = 1 the denominator is 1 − 1 = 0, so f(1) = 2/0 is undefined. Boxed Not defined (matches the key). (Note the value, not the limit: lim (x→1) (x³+1)/(x−1) does not exist either, since the numerator tends to 2.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q2(ii); book p484 = PDF p511; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: LHL is the value approached through x < a, RHL through x > a; the limit exists iff both exist and are equal.
questions.question: Q3. What is meant by the left-hand and right-hand limit of a function? State the condition for the limit to exist at a point. Prove that lim (x→0) |x| = 0 but lim (x→0) |x|/x does not exist.
questions.solution:
Definitions. lim (x→a⁻) f(x) = L means f(x) can be made arbitrarily close to L by taking x < a close enough to a; lim (x→a⁺) f(x) = M is the same with x > a. The two-sided limit exists iff both one-sided limits exist and are equal: lim (x→a) f(x) = L ⇔ lim (x→a⁻) f(x) = lim (x→a⁺) f(x) = L.
Proof 1: for x > 0, |x| = x → 0; for x < 0, |x| = −x → 0. Both one-sided limits are 0, so lim (x→0) |x| = 0.
Proof 2: for x > 0, |x|/x = 1, so the right limit is 1; for x < 0, |x|/x = −1, so the left limit is −1. Since 1 ≠ −1, the limit does not exist. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q3; book p484 = PDF p511

questions.knowledgeNote: The value f(a) is what the function assigns at a; the limit is what it approaches. They can differ (removable discontinuity).
questions.question: Q4. Distinguish between the limit and the value of a function at a point. Given f(x) = (ax + b)/(x + 1), lim (x→0) f(x) = 2 and lim (x→∞) f(x) = 1, prove that f(−2) = 0.
questions.solution:
Distinction. lim (x→a) f(x) describes the behaviour of f near a and ignores f(a) itself (f need not even be defined at a); f(a) is the single assigned value. A function is continuous at a exactly when the two coincide.
Now lim (x→0) (ax + b)/(x + 1) = (0 + b)/(0 + 1) = b = 2, so b = 2. And lim (x→∞) (ax + b)/(x + 1) = a (ratio of the leading coefficients) = 1, so a = 1. Then f(x) = (x + 2)/(x + 1) and f(−2) = (−2 + 2)/(−2 + 1) = 0/(−1) = 0. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q4; book p484 = PDF p511

questions.knowledgeNote: Two limits pin the two constants: the limit at 0 gives one equation, the limit at infinity the other.
questions.question: Q5. Define the limit of a function at a point. Given f(x) = (x + 6)/(cx − d), lim (x→0) f(x) = −6 and lim (x→∞) f(x) = 1/3, prove that f(13) = 1/2.
questions.solution:
Definition. L = lim (x→a) f(x) if for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that 0 < |x − a| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − L| < ε.
At x → 0: (x + 6)/(cx − d) → 6/(−d) = −6/d, so −6/d = −6 ⇒ d = 1. At x → ∞ the quotient tends to the ratio of leading coefficients, 1/c, so 1/c = 1/3 ⇒ c = 3. Hence f(x) = (x + 6)/(3x − 1) and f(13) = (13 + 6)/(39 − 1) = 19/38 = 1/2. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q5; book p484 = PDF p511

questions.knowledgeNote: Indeterminate forms 0/0, ∞/∞, ∞−∞, 0·∞, 0⁰, 1^∞, ∞⁰ need algebraic rewriting; here a conjugate removes ∞−∞.
questions.question: Q6. What is an indeterminate form? State their different forms. Evaluate lim (x→∞) √x(√x − √(x − a)). [T.U. 2052]
questions.solution:
An indeterminate form is an expression whose limiting value cannot be read off from the limits of its parts — the answer depends on how the parts approach their limits. The seven standard forms are 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞ − ∞, 0⁰, 1^∞ and ∞⁰.
Evaluation: √x − √(x − a) = [(x) − (x − a)]/[√x + √(x − a)] = a/[√x + √(x − a)], an ∞ − ∞ form removed by the conjugate. Multiply by √x: a√x/[√x + √(x − a)]. Divide top and bottom by √x: a/[1 + √(1 − a/x)] → a/(1 + 1) = a/2. Boxed a/2 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q6; book p484 = PDF p511; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: A function can be continuous nowhere yet still have a limit at a point where the nearby non-integer values all give 0.
questions.question: Q7. Let f: R → R be defined by f(x) = x if x is an integer, f(x) = 0 if x is not an integer. Find lim (x→1) f(x). Is it the same as f(1)?
questions.solution: Approach x = 1 through non-integers: then f(x) = 0 for every such x, so the limit along that path is 0. Approach through integers: the only integer arbitrarily close to 1 is 1 itself, so this does not produce other values and the two-sided limit is 0. Hence lim (x→1) f(x) = 0. But f(1) = 1 (1 is an integer). Since 0 ≠ 1, the limit is not the same as the value — f is discontinuous at x = 1. Boxed 0, No (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q7; book p484 = PDF p511; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: Combine the fractions over the factorised denominator; the 0/0 factor cancels.
questions.question: Q8(i). Prove that lim (x→3) [1/(x − 3) − 9/(x³ − 3x²)] = 2/3.
questions.solution: Write x³ − 3x² = x²(x − 3). Then 1/(x − 3) − 9/[x²(x − 3)] = [x² − 9]/[x²(x − 3)] = (x − 3)(x + 3)/[x²(x − 3)] = (x + 3)/x² for x ≠ 3. Therefore the limit is (3 + 3)/3² = 6/9 = 2/3. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q8(i); book p484 = PDF p511; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: The common denominator is (x − 3)(x + 3); the numerator then collapses to x(x − 3).
questions.question: Q8(ii). Prove that lim (x→3) [ (x² + 9)/(x² − 9) − 3/(x − 3) ] = 1/2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q8(ii); book p484 = PDF p511; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: Difference of powers rule: lim (x^n − a^n)/(x − a) = n·a^(n−1) holds for negative n too.
questions.question: Q9(i). Evaluate: lim (x→2) (x^(−3) − 2^(−3))/(x − 2).
questions.solution: This is the difference-of-powers limit with n = −3, a = 2: the limit is n·a^(n−1) = −3·2^(−4) = −3/16. Direct check: x^(−3) − 2^(−3) = (2³ − x³)/(8x³) = −(x − 2)(x² + 2x + 4)/(8x³), so the quotient → −(4 + 4 + 4)/(8·8) = −12/64 = −3/16. Boxed −3/16 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q9(i); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: At infinity only the leading terms matter: (2x)^6 and (3x)^4 over (2x)^10.
questions.question: Q9(ii). Evaluate: lim (x→∞) (2x − 1)^6 (3x − 1)^4/(2x + 1)^10.
questions.solution: In the numerator the dominant term is (2x)^6(3x)^4 = 2^6·3^4·x^10; in the denominator it is (2x)^10 = 2^10·x^10. The quotient tends to 2^6·3^4/2^10 = 3^4/2^4 = 81/16. Boxed 81/16 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q9(ii); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: Substitute u = 1 + x; both numerator and denominator are then differences of powers divided by x = u − 1.
questions.question: Q9(iii). Evaluate: lim (x→0) [(1 + x)^6 − 1]/[(1 + x)² − 1].
questions.solution: Divide numerator and denominator by x: [((1+x)^6 − 1)/x] ÷ [((1+x)² − 1)/x]. With u = 1 + x → 1, each quotient is a difference-of-powers limit: (u^6 − 1)/(u − 1) → 6 and (u² − 1)/(u − 1) → 2. Ratio = 6/2 = 3. Boxed 3 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q9(iii); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: Difference of powers with a fractional exponent: (u^(5/2) − c^(5/2))/(u − c) → (5/2)c^(3/2).
questions.question: Q9(iv). Evaluate: lim (x→a) [(x + 2)^(5/2) − (a + 2)^(5/2)]/(x − a).
questions.solution: Put u = x + 2 and c = a + 2, so x − a = u − c and the quotient becomes (u^(5/2) − c^(5/2))/(u − c). Writing u = c + h and expanding by the binomial theorem, (c + h)^(5/2) = c^(5/2) + (5/2)c^(3/2)h + …, so the quotient → (5/2)c^(3/2) = (5/2)(a + 2)^(3/2). Boxed (5/2)(a + 2)^(3/2) (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q9(iv); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: (x³ − a³)/(x − a) → 3a², so a single given limit becomes an equation in a.
questions.question: Q10. If lim (x→a) (x³ − a³)/(x − a) = 27, find all possible values of a.
questions.solution: x³ − a³ = (x − a)(x² + ax + a²), so the quotient is x² + ax + a² → a² + a² + a² = 3a². The condition 3a² = 27 gives a² = 9, hence a = 3 or a = −3. Boxed a = ±3 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q10; book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: Degrees must be converted to radians before using sin θ/θ → 1: x° = πx/180.
questions.question: Q11(i). Find the limiting value of lim (x→0) sin x°/x.
questions.solution: The symbol x° means x degrees = πx/180 radians. So sin x°/x = sin(πx/180)/x = (π/180)·sin(πx/180)/(πx/180) → (π/180)·1 = π/180. Boxed π/180 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q11(i); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: Ratio of two 1 − cos forms: (4θ)²/2 over (6θ)²/2.
questions.question: Q11(ii). Find the limiting value of lim (θ→0) (1 − cos 4θ)/(1 − cos 6θ).
questions.solution: Write 1 − cos 4θ = 2 sin²2θ and 1 − cos 6θ = 2 sin²3θ. Ratio = [sin 2θ/2θ]²·(2θ)² ÷ {[sin 3θ/3θ]²·(3θ)²} → 4θ²/9θ² = 4/9. Boxed 4/9 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q11(ii); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: With t = π/2 − x, cos x = sin t and the denominator becomes t.
questions.question: Q11(iii). Find the limiting value of lim (x→π/2) cos x/(π/2 − x).
questions.solution: Put t = π/2 − x → 0, so x = π/2 − t and cos x = cos(π/2 − t) = sin t. The quotient becomes sin t/t → 1. Boxed 1 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q11(iii); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: Near 0, tan 2x ≈ 2x and sin x ≈ x, so the leading terms decide the limit.
questions.question: Q11(iv). Find the limiting value of lim (x→0) (tan 2x − x)/(3x − sin x).
questions.solution: Divide top and bottom by x: [tan 2x/x − 1]/[3 − sin x/x]. Now tan 2x/x = 2·tan 2x/(2x) → 2 and sin x/x → 1. The limit is (2 − 1)/(3 − 1) = 1/2. Boxed 1/2 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q11(iv); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: Shift to the singular point: with t = π − x, sin(x/2) = cos(t/2) and 1 − cos(t/2) ≈ t²/8.
questions.question: Q11(v). Find the limiting value of lim (x→π) (1 − sin(x/2))/(π − x)².
questions.solution: Put t = π − x → 0, so x = π − t and x/2 = π/2 − t/2, hence sin(x/2) = cos(t/2). Numerator: 1 − cos(t/2) = 2 sin²(t/4). Quotient = 2 sin²(t/4)/t² = 2·(1/16)·[sin(t/4)/(t/4)]² → 2/16 = 1/8. Boxed 1/8 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q11(v); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: With u = π − 2x, cos 2x = −cos u, so 1 + cos 2x = 1 − cos u ≈ u²/2.
questions.question: Q11(vi). Find the limiting value of lim (x→π/2) (1 + cos 2x)/(π − 2x)².
questions.solution: Put u = π − 2x → 0, so 2x = π − u and cos 2x = cos(π − u) = −cos u. Then 1 + cos 2x = 1 − cos u = 2 sin²(u/2). Quotient = 2 sin²(u/2)/u² = (1/2)[sin(u/2)/(u/2)]² → 1/2. Boxed 1/2 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q11(vi); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: sin(1/x) oscillates between −1 and +1 however close x gets to 0: no limit.
questions.question: Q11(vii). Find the limiting value of lim (x→0) sin(1/x).
questions.solution: Take xₙ = 1/(π/2 + 2nπ) → 0⁺: sin(1/xₙ) = sin(π/2 + 2nπ) = 1 for every n. Take yₙ = 1/(3π/2 + 2nπ) → 0⁺: sin(1/yₙ) = −1. Two sequences tending to 0 give different limits (1 and −1), so the limit does not exist. Boxed does not exist (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q11(vii); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: Squeeze theorem: |x sin(1/x)| ≤ |x| → 0, so the oscillation is crushed.
questions.question: Q11(viii). Find the limiting value of lim (x→0) x sin(1/x).
questions.solution: For x ≠ 0, −1 ≤ sin(1/x) ≤ 1, so −|x| ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ |x|. Both bounds tend to 0 as x → 0, hence by the squeeze theorem the limit is 0. Boxed 0 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q11(viii); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: Split into (sin x − sin a)/(x − a) and (x − a)/(√x − √a) = √x + √a.
questions.question: Q11(ix). Find the limiting value of lim (x→a) (sin x − sin a)/(√x − √a).
questions.solution: Rationalise the denominator: √x − √a = (x − a)/(√x + √a). So the quotient = [(sin x − sin a)/(x − a)]·(√x + √a). Since (sin x − sin a)/(x − a) = 2 cos((x+a)/2)·sin((x−a)/2)/(x−a) → cos a, the limit is cos a·(√a + √a) = 2√a·cos a. Boxed 2√a cos a (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q11(ix); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: With t = a − x, tan(πx/2a) = cot(πt/2a) ≈ 2a/(πt), and the t cancels.
questions.question: Q11(x). Find the limiting value of lim (x→a) (a − x) tan(πx/2a).
questions.solution: Put t = a − x → 0, so x = a − t and πx/2a = π/2 − πt/(2a). Then tan(πx/2a) = cot(πt/(2a)) = cos(πt/2a)/sin(πt/2a). The expression = t·cos(πt/2a)/sin(πt/2a) = [πt/(2a)]/sin(πt/2a)·(2a/π)·cos(πt/2a) → 1·(2a/π)·1 = 2a/π. Boxed 2a/π (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q11(x); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: This is the difference quotient of g(t) = t sec t at t = x, so the limit is g′(x).
questions.question: Q11(xi). Find the limiting value of lim (y→0) [(x + y) sec(x + y) − x sec x]/y.
questions.solution: The quotient has the form [g(x + y) − g(x)]/y with g(t) = t sec t, so the limit is g′(x) = sec x + x·sec x tan x (product rule, (sec t)′ = sec t tan t). Equivalently expand: (x + y)sec(x + y) − x sec x = y sec(x + y) + x[sec(x + y) − sec x]; dividing by y and letting y → 0 gives sec x + x·x′(0) where the bracket derivative is sec x tan x. Boxed sec x + x sec x tan x (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q11(xi); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: At a join, substitute each branch and compare.
questions.question: Q12(i). f(x) = 3x² + 2 if x < 1, f(x) = 2x + 3 if x ≥ 1. Find lim (x→1) f(x).
questions.solution: Left limit (x < 1 rule): 3(1)² + 2 = 5. Right limit (x ≥ 1 rule): 2(1) + 3 = 5. Both agree, so the limit is 5. Boxed 5 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q12(i); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: Three-branch function: check each join separately; a mismatched pair means no limit there.
questions.question: Q12(ii). f(x) = 3 + 2x for −3/2 ≤ x < 0, f(x) = 3 − 2x for 0 ≤ x < 3/2, f(x) = −3 − 2x for x ≥ 3/2. Find lim (x→0) f(x) and lim (x→3/2) f(x) if they exist.
questions.solution: At x = 0: left branch 3 + 2x → 3; right branch 3 − 2x → 3. Equal, so lim (x→0) f(x) = 3. At x = 3/2: left branch 3 − 2x → 3 − 3 = 0; right branch −3 − 2x → −3 − 3 = −6. Since 0 ≠ −6, lim (x→3/2) f(x) does not exist. Boxed 3; does not exist (matches the key: '3, does not exist').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q12(ii); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: (e^(px) − 1)/(e^(qx) − 1): divide top and bottom by x and use (e^u − 1)/u → 1.
questions.question: Q13(a). Evaluate: lim (x→0) (e^(px) − 1)/(e^(qx) − 1).
questions.solution: Divide numerator and denominator by x: [(e^(px) − 1)/x] ÷ [(e^(qx) − 1)/x] = [p·(e^(px) − 1)/(px)] ÷ [q·(e^(qx) − 1)/(qx)] → p/q. Boxed p/q (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q13(a); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: e^x − e^(−x) ≈ 2x near 0; the extra +x makes the numerator 3x.
questions.question: Q13(b). Evaluate: lim (x→0) (e^x − e^(−x) + x)/x.
questions.solution: Split: (e^x − e^(−x))/x + 1. Now (e^x − e^(−x))/x = (e^x − 1)/x + (1 − e^(−x))/x = (e^x − 1)/x + (e^(−x) − 1)/(−x) → 1 + 1 = 2. Hence the limit is 2 + 1 = 3. Boxed 3 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q13(b); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: (a^x − 1)/x → log a and (b^x − 1)/x → log b; the ratio is the quotient of the logs.
questions.question: Q13(c). Evaluate: lim (x→0) (a^x − 1)/(b^x − 1).
questions.solution: Divide top and bottom by x: [(a^x − 1)/x]/[(b^x − 1)/x] → log a/log b. Boxed log a/log b (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q13(c); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: (2^x − 1)/x → log 2 while sin x/x → 1: split the quotient into two standard limits.
questions.question: Q14(a). Evaluate: lim (x→0) (2^x − 1)/sin x.
questions.solution: Write it as [(2^x − 1)/x]·[x/sin x] → (log 2)·1 = log 2. Boxed log 2 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q14(a); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: With u = sin x, e^u − 1 − u ≈ u²/2, so the numerator is of order x² and the x in the denominator wins.
questions.question: Q14(b). Evaluate: lim (x→0) (e^(sin x) − sin x − 1)/x.
questions.solution: Put u = sin x → 0. Then e^u = 1 + u + u²/2 + …, so e^u − u − 1 = u²/2 + O(u³). Since u = sin x ~ x, the numerator behaves like x²/2 and the whole quotient like x/2 → 0. Boxed 0 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q14(b); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: With t = π/2 − x, cos x = sin t, and (e^(sin t) − 1)/t → 1.
questions.question: Q14(c). Evaluate: lim (x→π/2) (e^(cos x) − 1)/(π/2 − x).
questions.solution: Put t = π/2 − x → 0, so cos x = cos(π/2 − t) = sin t. The quotient becomes (e^(sin t) − 1)/t = [(e^(sin t) − 1)/sin t]·(sin t/t) → 1·1 = 1. Boxed 1 (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q14(c); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486

questions.knowledgeNote: log x − log e = log(x/e) and log(1 + h)/h → 1 with h = (x − e)/e.
questions.question: Q14(d). Evaluate: lim (x→e) (log x − 1)/(x − e).
questions.solution: Since log e = 1, write log x − 1 = log(x/e). Put x = e(1 + h), so x − e = eh and h → 0. Then log(x/e) = log(1 + h), and the quotient = log(1 + h)/(eh) = (1/e)·[log(1 + h)/h] → (1/e)·1 = 1/e. Boxed 1/e (matches the key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.16 Additional Questions (Limits) Q14(d); book p485 = PDF p512; key book p486
